Chapter 1: The Power of Incentives—Why People Do What They Do
Every day, you and I make choices that seem straightforward—like picking a job, figuring out how to spend our money, or deciding the best way to raise our kids. But underneath all those decisions, there’s this quiet force working in the background. It’s the world of incentives—rewards and penalties, both the ones we spot right away and the ones that slip by unnoticed, nudging us toward some behaviors and away from others.
Picture this: a teacher stands at the front of a classroom, feeling the weight of those standardized tests coming up. The school’s reputation? Funding? Even the teacher’s own job—yep, all riding on how well those kids do. In that moment, the teacher faces a real crossroads. Should they work overtime to help students learn more? Or, just maybe, cut a few corners to boost those scores? The pull to succeed is strong, but so is the temptation to bend the rules.
Now, let’s travel halfway across the world, where a group of sumo wrestlers is gearing up for a make-or-break match. For these athletes, every win and loss carves their reputation. The difference between a winning season and a losing one? It can mean everything—from deep respect to outright disgrace. And sometimes, the pressure leads to quiet deals—like letting someone else win today in exchange for a favor down the road. The fans cheer, never guessing there might be more at play than just skill and strength.
What do these stories have in common? They show us something most people miss: incentives shape our actions everywhere—not just in business or economics. These nudges can be about money, social standing, or even our sense of right and wrong. Sometimes, they inspire honesty and hard work. Other times, they make room for cheating, deception, or consequences nobody expected.
Here’s another example—real estate agents. When you’re selling your house, you probably trust your agent to get you the best deal. But think about it—the agent’s commission is just a small slice of the price. So, whether your home sells for a little more or less doesn’t really change their paycheck that much. For you, though, every extra dollar counts. This subtle mismatch means agents might suggest you accept lower offers just to wrap things up quickly and move on to the next client. Their main incentive? Closing more deals, not necessarily squeezing every last dollar from yours.
But incentives aren’t always bad news—they can be designed to help people do the right thing. Cities try to cut crime by offering rewards for turning in illegal guns. Companies hand out bonuses when employees hit their targets. Parents promise treats to kids who finish their homework. Sounds great, right? But sometimes, these good intentions backfire. There’s a famous story about a daycare that started fining parents for picking up their kids late. What happened? Instead of showing up on time, more parents started running late. The fine turned away the guilt and made it feel like just another payment—they could simply buy themselves extra time.
So, what’s the real takeaway here? Incentives are everywhere, shaping the choices you and I make—big and small. They can push us toward honesty or open the door to cheating. They can bring people together or leave them feeling resentful. And most of us react to these incentives, even when we don’t realize it. Sometimes, it’s the ones we never notice that steer our decisions the most—quietly, behind the scenes.
